questions.question: Explain how colonialism contributed to differences in development between countries.
questions.expected_answer: European powers colonised most of Africa (Berlin Conference 1884-85; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent) and organised colonies to export raw materials and buy manufactured goods. Forced cash-crop production and labour (e.g. rubber in Leopold's Congo), railways from mines to ports rather than between colonies, limited education and health services, land seizure and arbitrary borders left export-dependent economies, weak infrastructure, few skilled people and sometimes conflict at independence.

questions.question: Explain how unfair trade affects developing countries, using the terms of trade.
questions.expected_answer: Many developing countries depend on exporting primary products (Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire about 60 per cent of cocoa; Zambia copper). Prices are volatile and tend to rise more slowly than manufactured goods: if coffee falls from 3 000 to 2 000 dollars a tonne, a 60 000-dollar tractor costs 30 instead of 20 tonnes, worsening terms of trade. Most value is added elsewhere (farmers get about 6 per cent of a chocolate bar). Tariff escalation and rich-country farm subsidies add to the disadvantage. Responses: Fairtrade, AfCFTA, local processing.

questions.question: Explain the role of technology and industrialisation in development, with reference to South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Industrialisation, from Britain's Industrial Revolution (1760s), raised productivity, incomes and tax revenue; early industrialisers gained wealth and power, while late or colonised countries struggled (Indian textiles declined); the Asian Tigers and China industrialised rapidly. Today's digital divide limits access to online opportunities. South Africa industrialised from diamonds (1867) and gold (1886), relying on migrant labour, then Iscor (1928) and Sasol (1950), but benefits were racially unequal and minerals still dominate exports.
